title: Mark Making
strapline: Every scribble is a sentence waiting to happen — big arms first, pencil grips later.
intent: Build the physical foundations of writing in the right order: shoulder, then elbow, then wrist, then fingers
Let grips develop at each child's pace — from fist to fingers to an effective tripod, without forcing any stage
Discover that marks carry meaning: naming them, narrating them, and separating "drawing" from "writing"
Write for real purposes inside play — shopping lists, signs, birthday cards, appointments at the vet's
Travel the name journey: recognising it, finding its first letter everywhere, and one day writing it
Notice print doing jobs all around the room and the neighbourhood
implementation: Offer big-arm mark making daily — chalk on the wall, decorating brushes and water on the fence, ribbon sticks in the air — this is where pencil control actually starts
Put mark making everywhere, not at one table: clipboards in the construction area, notepads by the home-corner phone, chalk in the garden
Watch grips without correcting; offer chunky and triangular tools where they help, and note the fist-to-fingers shift in your observations
Take dictation often — "tell me what your writing says" — and scribe the child's words underneath their marks
Use name cards at self-registration and model name writing letter by letter, celebrating the first letter first
Create real audiences: cards that get posted, party invitations that get answered, a "please do not knock down" sign for the block area
Write aloud in front of children — the snack list, the register, a label for the shelf — so they see writing doing real jobs
key_questions: Would you like to tell me what your writing says?
Shall we make a sign so everybody knows?
What do we need to put on our list?
Whose name starts the same as yours?
Which pen makes your favourite kind of line?

impact.text: Our youngest mark makers work from the shoulder — big loops, stabs and sweeps with a whole-arm, fisted grip.
Children make marks freely and give them meaning after the fact: "that's a dinosaur", said with total conviction.
Grips move from fist towards fingers, and snipping with scissors strengthens the same small muscles.
Children draw with intent — "it's mummy" — narrating the picture as it grows, and start pointing at some marks saying "that's my writing".
Children spot print doing jobs: their name card at registration, the logo on the cereal box, the sign on the door.
Letter-like shapes appear, children have a go at their own name, and lists, cards and tickets get "written" all over the role play.
Drawing happens with a comfortable, effective grip that can steer the pencil where the idea wants to go.
Older children write their name and make marks with meaning they can communicate — labels for models, signs for dens, cards for friends.

enhancements: Decorating brushes and buckets of water for giant disappearing letters on the playground slabs
Clipboards and pencils tucked into every area — construction, home corner, garden, book corner
Old diaries, receipt pads, calendars and envelopes in the home corner so writing has real jobs
A shallow tray of sand or salt for finger writing — mistakes shake away
Ribbon sticks and streamers for sky-writing big shapes and letter movements
Name cards with photos at the making table, laminated for tracing fingers over
A real post box (and a weekly walk to the real real one) so cards and letters actually go somewhere

playing_exploring: Mark making tools sit inside every kind of play, so writing starts as part of the game, not a task
Children choose their surface and tool — wall, floor, air, sand — and find their own favourite lines
active_learning: The name journey is powered by the child's own drive — nobody works harder at a word than a child writing their name
creating_thinking: Children work out for themselves that marks can stand for sounds, words and ideas — the deepest symbol-thinking there is
They invent their own systems first — strings of letter-like shapes with serious meaning — before conventional writing arrives
